drug_class: ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis) Agent / Glutamate Blocker (Neuroprotective)
purpose: Riluzole is used to treat ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig's disease. It does not cure ALS, but it can help slow down how fast the disease gets worse and may help you live longer. It is currently one of the standard treatments prescribed for this condition.
how_it_works: In ALS, certain brain chemicals called glutamate build up to harmful levels and damage nerve cells. Riluzole works by reducing the amount of glutamate activity in your brain and spinal cord. By lowering this harmful buildup, it helps protect your nerve cells from dying as quickly.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, dizziness, tiredness or weakness, stomach pain, loss of appetite, and tingling or numbness around the mouth or fingers. Some people may also notice a slight increase in their liver enzymes, which is why regular blood tests are important.
warnings: Riluzole can sometimes cause liver problems, so your doctor will check your liver with blood tests regularly — especially in the first few months. Tell your doctor right away if you notice yellowing of your skin or eyes, unusual tiredness, or dark urine. Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medication as it can increase the risk of liver damage. Also tell your doctor about all other medications you take, since some can interact with riluzole.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 50 mg taken by mouth twice a day, about 12 hours apart. It works best when taken on an empty stomach — at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal. Try to take it at the same times each day to keep a steady level in your body.
